**Wetware computing: living neurons do tasks, but who does the work?**

Synthetic biological intelligence grows neurons or small brain-like organoids on electrode arrays and tries to use them as computers, by stimulating them and reading their activity.

**Where it stands.** Results are real but narrow. Neuron cultures have shown altered network activity in closed-loop tasks such as the Pong game, and a 2025 [Braille-recognition study with organoids](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.20850) (FinalSpark and Bristol) classified tactile patterns. The open worry is attribution: much of the performance can come from the stimulation code and the conventional classifier that reads the signals, not from the tissue.

**What an outsider can use.** FinalSpark's [Neuroplatform](https://finalspark.com/neuroplatform/) sells remote access to living organoids with a Python interface; reported pricing was about $1,000 a month in 2025, to be confirmed. Cortical Labs' CL1, a [purchasable biological computer](https://spectrum.ieee.org/biological-computer-for-sale), was reported at $35,000.

**Outside the US.** FinalSpark is in Switzerland and the Braille work includes Bristol, UK.

**What the lab could test.** Train the same classifier on the stimulus alone and on the recorded response, to see what the tissue adds.

Checked 28 November 2026; first pass. Prices and results are as reported, not verified by us.
